name: Leg raise
cue: Raise your straight legs to hip height, then lower them slowly.
research: Straight-leg raise in the captain's chair (vertical knee raise station), the harder progression of the knee raise: the longer lever of the nearly straight legs raises the hip-flexion moment the abdominals must hold the pelvis against. Station, hang and grip are exactly those of exercises/knee_raise.json (parts copied by tools/design/leg_raise.mjs): upper back pinned on the vertical back pad, shoulders depressed, upper arms vertical under the shoulders, forearms on the horizontal pads (elbows ~86-90), neutral grip on the vertical handles; the feet hang 26 cm clear of the base. Hip flexion 5 -> 86 (thighs 96 deg from hanging, legs at hip height), knees 5 -> 9 (nearly straight), ankles -15; in the last part of the rise the pelvis rolls into a slight posterior tilt (10 deg: lumbar flexion 12 against the pelvis, thoracolumbar extension 2, spinal flexion 0 -> 10) while the thorax stays vertical on the pad, so the low back presses toward the pad (lumbar_back gap 0.0060 -> 0.0043 H). The hips move only through that tilt (hip-to-C7 chord -5.4 -> -6.4 deg): no swing. The return uncurls the pelvis first (via key N), then lowers the legs over the slow eccentric. Sources: ExRx (vertical / captain's chair leg raise: the hip flexors raise the legs while the abdominals hold the pelvis, and only a posterior pelvic tilt at the top makes the abs shorten); Jeff Nippard (leg raises for a lower-abs bias, the Roman / captain's chair preferred to hanging because the back stays locked against the pad, and no momentum); the ACE-sponsored San Diego State abdominal EMG study (2001: the captain's chair among the top exercises for the rectus abdominis and the obliques); Andersson, Ma and Thorstensson 1998 (Scand J Rehabil Med 30:175-83: leg raises drive the iliacus and rectus femoris hardest while the abdominals stabilise the pelvis). Primary: rectus abdominis; secondary: the hip flexors (iliopsoas proxy at the femoral triangle and the proximal rectus femoris, head rect_fem_up), as in the knee raise but one tier lower. Geometry: tools/design/leg_raise.mjs.

targets.note: trunk_flexion here is the thorax tilt (the back stays on the pad, 0 throughout); the slight posterior pelvic tilt at the top is checked as spinal_flexion (0 -> 10) and the hip-to-C7 chord (trunk_chord 0 -> -3).

camera.note: Research view as for the knee raise (az 70 / el 5), turned 10 deg toward the front and raised 20 deg (az 60 / el 25, 22.4 deg in all). Looking down over the raised legs keeps the rectus in view at the peak, above the thighs, and shows the whole rectus plus the hip flexors (amber, front of the hips) at the stretch: phone stage glow about 1000 CSS px at the stretch and 630 at the peak. The knee raise view (az 50 / el 25) shows ~20 % more glow but puts the near vertical handle of the shared station across the lower abs; from az 60 the handle stands beside them. At the peak the hip flexors fold into the hip crease, so the secondary shows from the stretch through the first half of the lift and again in the lowering.
